USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Take the negotiation now opening in Beijing (Mnuchin/Lighthizer/Kudlow vs. Liu He) and use the outstanding tariff threat as leverage to secure a package of structural concessions — tech-transfer curbs, financial-sector opening, auto-tariff cuts, and a meaningful reduction in the ~$375B goods deficit — without triggering the $50B tariffs or threatening a further $100B round. Do not unilaterally escalate while talks are live, and do not roll back leverage (ZTE denial, proposed list) prematurely. Hold the line, demand concrete deliverables, and only turn the screws if Beijing stalls.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is mild-to-favorable rather than existential. The US holds the initiative: it published the $50B Section 301 list (timeline 2018-04-03), banned ZTE (2018-04-16), and threatened an additional $100B, while no US tariff on Chinese goods is actually in force — the comment window runs to May 22 and implementation is conditional on negotiations (Politico/US News, 2018-04/05-02). Macro fundamentals support that favorable reading: industrial production rose (INDPRO +0.9% over the window to 102.4), UMich consumer sentiment held at ~98, and the broad dollar firmed to ~110, so the dispute is not yet biting. That said, the reading is tempered rather than a clean 'opportunity' anchor because China has targeted the farm belt the US needs for the 2018 midterms — soybeans (~$14B/yr, roughly half of US soybean exports) plus pork, sorghum and aircraft on the April 4 retaliation list — hitting an already-depressed farm income (CNBC/US News/Mercury News, 2018-03-15 to 04-07), and credit conditions are tightening (Baa yield to ~4.8%, 10yr near 3.0%). Hence threat_score of roughly -0.3 (favorable terrain and leverage, but genuine escalation downside). The action stance reflects that the opportunity is best captured at the table, not by pulling the trigger: escalading further risks a retaliatory spiral that lands hardest on US farmers and consumers, while conceding now would squander hard-won leverage. With Xi already signalling openness (auto-tariff reductions) and both sides' penalties explicitly contingent on the talks' outcome, 'negotiate' — maintain the threat as leverage, extract concessions, avoid both unilateral escalation and premature rollback — is the value-maximizing move at this decision date.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the Beijing talks with the US delegation seriously and use them to stabilize the situation — offer limited, non-structural concessions (increased purchases of US goods, further market-access opening) to buy time and de-escalate, while refusing to dismantle Made in China 2025 and pressing for relief on the ZTE denial order. Hold our proposed $50B retaliation (incl. soybeans) in reserve as leverage rather than expanding it now. Do not capitulate to numerical trade-balance or structural demands, but signal genuine willingness to negotiate rather than walking away.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high (0.6). The Section 301 list published Apr 3 targets the aerospace/ICT/robotics core of Made in China 2025 (timeline), Trump has threatened a further ~$100B (chinausfocus), and the Apr 16 ZTE seven-year export denial is a 'precise munition' that cripples a flagship telecom maker and exposes China's hard dependency on US chips and Android (timeline; LA Times 5/1; Reuters 4/16); Huawei is under similar investigation so this is systemic firm-level targeting, not an isolated case. That is firm-level targeting plus a structural challenge to our tech self-sufficiency goals — toward the high anchor. But it is not existential: tariffs are still only proposed (comment period open), talks are opening now, our economy and reserves remain strong, and we hold counter-leverage (soybeans, autos, aircraft). Hence 0.6, not 1.0. On action, the correct response to this high-threat moment is disciplined de-escalation through the talks that begin today (5/3): escalating tariff retaliation now, when the US delegation is in Beijing and Trump has already telegraphed another $100B, risks an uncontrolled trade war that would damage our own export and tech-supply sectors more than it punishes Washington. Holding firm on core industrial-policy sovereignty while signaling openness — negotiate (0.1) — is the posture that keeps the door open without conceding the strategic high ground.
